beats.say: In 1978, a Formula 1 car won its very first race. Easily. And it never raced again.
Socho. Jeetne wali car ko hi garage mein band kar diya.
beats.cap: Think about it. They locked the winning car away in the garage.

beats.say: This is the story of F1's banned tricks. Six ideas so clever, the sport had to stop them. And the last twist? It's now in the rulebook.
lines: and the last twist is now the rule

beats.say: Sweden, 1978. Brabham's designer, Gordon Murray, put a giant fan on the back of his car.
lines: on the back of the car

beats.say: Officially, it was there to cool the engine.
Lekin asli kaam kuch aur tha. Woh fan car ke neeche se hawa kheench leta tha.
beats.cap: But its real job was something else. It sucked the air out from under the car.

beats.say: That pulled the car down onto the track, so it could corner faster. Niki Lauda won the Swedish Grand Prix with it.
Rival teams were furious. Brabham's boss, Bernie Ecclestone, needed their support, so he withdrew the car after one race. The win still stands.
Two years earlier, Tyrrell tried something even stranger. A car with six wheels.
Four tiny front wheels sat behind the front wing, so less air hit them.
But small tyres grip less. So they used two pairs instead of one.
Aur yeh mazaak nahi tha. Sweden, 1976 mein, Tyrrell first aur second aaye.
beats.cap: And this was no joke. In Sweden in 1976, Tyrrell finished first and second.

beats.say: It's still the only six-wheeled car ever to win a Grand Prix. Six-wheelers never came back.
Jump to 2005. Inside the nose of the Renault sat a weight, mounted on springs.
When the car went over bumps, the weight moved the other way and calmed the car down. So the tyres kept their grip.
In 2006, the stewards in Germany said it was legal. But the FIA appealed against its own stewards, and the device was banned.
Renault had to remove it in the middle of the season. Even so, Renault won both championships.
